title: Reading Isaiah

objectives.can: Read a chapter of Isaiah, handling its poetry, rare words and long sentences.

explanation.summary: Isaiah is the largest of the prophetic books and one of the hardest, with long sentences, rare words and a mixture of prose and poetry. Chapter 6 is a good first reading: a vision told by the prophet in the first person, with a famous song of the seraphim. This lesson reads Isaiah 6:1–8 and ends with a table of its commoner words.

sections.heading: What you will meet in Isaiah
body: The book of Isaiah is mostly poetry: oracles in parallel lines, with a wide vocabulary, images, and sentences that run on for several lines. Parts of it are prose, including some narrative about Hezekiah. Chapter 6 is a prose report of a vision, spoken by Isaiah himself, with poetry inside it in the seraphim's song and in the LORD's words.

The passage for this lesson is Isaiah 6:1–8, the vision of the LORD in the temple and the prophet's cleansing and answer. The rest of the chapter is 6:9–13, the commission itself. There the LORD tells Isaiah to say words that harden the people, in a famous and difficult passage. It begins with a command that uses an infinitive absolute beside an imperative, as in שִׁמְעוּ שָׁמוֹעַ in 6:9. After this lesson you can read it yourself, and you may then choose your books freely in the Reading section.

sections.heading: A vision told in the first person
body: Isaiah tells the vision in wayyiqtol verbs in the first person singular: וָאֶרְאֶה, 'and I saw' (6:1), וָאֹמַר, 'and I said' (6:5), וָאֶשְׁמַע, 'and I heard' (6:8). They have the same form as the third person wayyiqtol, but the prefix is א and the meaning is the speaker's own. The story is told from inside.

The scene is set in the first verse with a date, a time phrase built of construct chains: בִּשְׁנַת מוֹת הַמֶּלֶךְ עֻזִּיָּהוּ, 'in the year of the death of King Uzziah'. After the verb of seeing the object is introduced with אֶת, and the participle יֹשֵׁב, 'sitting', and the adjectives רָם and נִשָּׂא describe what the prophet saw. Then the clause וְשׁוּלָיו מְלֵאִים אֶת הַהֵיכָל adds his hem, filling the temple. A suffix on the noun, -ָיו, refers back to אֲדֹנָי.

sections.heading: Participles, repeated actions and numbers
body: In 6:2 the seraphim are described with a participle, עֹמְדִים, 'standing', and then in a distributive sentence: שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַיִם שֵׁשׁ כְּנָפַיִם לְאֶחָד, 'six wings, six wings, to each one'. Each use of a wing is told in a yiqtol with בִּשְׁתַּיִם: בִּשְׁתַּיִם יְכַסֶּה פָנָיו, 'with two he covers his face'. The yiqtol here is not a future. It describes what each seraph does, again and again; a reader can think of it as the state of things in the vision.
Notice the numbers: the dual כְּנָפַיִם for 'wings' (a pair), the numeral שֵׁשׁ, and בִּשְׁתַּיִם, 'with two', where ב means 'with, by means of'.

sections.heading: The song and its famous line
body: Verse 3 begins with וְקָרָא זֶה אֶל זֶה וְאָמַר, 'and one called to another, and said'. The two weqatal verbs continue the description of what happened again and again in the vision, and זֶה … זֶה is 'one … another'. Then comes the song, set out in short lines: קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת, and מְלֹא כָל הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ.

The last line has no verb. It is a nominal clause. A common reading takes מְלֹא כָל הָאָרֶץ, 'the fullness of all the earth', as the predicate and כְּבוֹדוֹ, 'his glory', as the subject: 'the whole earth's fullness is his glory'. Other renderings are possible, such as 'the whole earth is full of his glory'. The grammar allows more than one rendering, and we note this and read the line as it stands. The word צְבָאוֹת is a plural noun used as part of a title, and a table below glosses it as 'army; war'.

sections.heading: Rare words and hard places
body: Isaiah 6 has rare words. In 6:6 the words רִצְפָּה and בְּמֶלְקַחַיִם, 'glowing stone' and 'tongs', occur very few times in the Bible. A reader will meet such words often in Isaiah and does well to read for the sense of the whole line. The seraphim, שְׂרָפִים, appear in the Bible only a few times, and the word is related to a root meaning 'burn'.

In 6:5 the verb נִדְמֵיתִי is a Niphal of a root that dictionaries and translators read in different ways: 'I am undone, I am destroyed' or 'I am silenced'. The following clause with כִּי gives the reason, and the exact word does not change that structure. In 6:7 the verb תְּכֻפָּר is Pual, a passive: your sin is covered or expiated, with no agent named.

Verse 6:5 also shows a construct chain with an adjective, אִישׁ טְמֵא שְׂפָתַיִם, 'a man unclean of lips'. The adjective is in the construct state, and the dual noun שְׂפָתַיִם after it says in what respect he is unclean.

sections.heading: Commoner words in this passage
body: The passage contains a number of fairly common words that earlier lessons of this course have not listed. They are gathered in the table below, in the form in which they stand in the passage, with the gloss that the analysis of the text gives. Learn them as a group: most of them recur through the prophets and the psalms.
Read the table once, then read the passage again. A gloss is a pointer, not a definition: where it gives two senses, the context chooses.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read 6:1–8 as three movements: the vision (verses 1–4), the prophet's cry and cleansing (verses 5–7), and the call and the answer (verse 8). In each, find the speaker. Mark the first person verbs, the participles that describe, and the speeches. Look up words only after trying the line.

misunderstandings: Reading וָאֶרְאֶה as a third person verb. The prefix א marks the first person singular, 'I'.
Reading the yiqtol יְכַסֶּה as a future. In this description it tells what each seraph does, again and again.
Supplying 'is' in a nominal clause as if the Hebrew were missing a word. The line about the glory of the earth is complete without a verb.
Treating a rare word as an error. Isaiah uses unusual words on purpose, and their sense often comes from the line they stand in.

deeper.heading: The threefold holy
body: The repetition of קָדוֹשׁ three times is an example of how Hebrew can mark intensity by repeating a word. Other examples are in the Psalms and the Prophets. Interpreters have discussed for a long time what the threefold form means, and the grammar can say only that the word is repeated and is predicate to the name that follows.

paradigms.title: Commoner words of Isaiah 6:1–8
paradigms.caption: Each word is given as it stands in the passage; the gloss is the one given by the analysis of the text.

examples.analysis: A date in a construct chain, בִּשְׁנַת מוֹת הַמֶּלֶךְ עֻזִּיָּהוּ, then the first person wayyiqtol וָאֶרְאֶה, 'and I saw'. The participle יֹשֵׁב describes אֲדֹנָי, and the suffix of וְשׁוּלָיו points back to him.

examples.analysis: Two weqatal verbs, וְקָרָא and וְאָמַר, with זֶה אֶל זֶה, 'one to another'. The song: the repeated adjective קָדוֹשׁ and the title יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת, then a nominal clause with no verb, מְלֹא כָל הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ.

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: Then said I: Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts.

examples.analysis: Isaiah answers the vision: וָאֹמַר is a first person wayyiqtol. The cry אוֹי לִי, 'woe to me', is followed by נִדְמֵיתִי, a Niphal qatal whose exact sense is debated, and a כִּי clause giving the reason: אִישׁ טְמֵא שְׂפָתַיִם אָנֹכִי, with the adjective in the construct state before the dual noun.

examples.analysis: The seraph touches Isaiah's mouth with the Hiphil wayyiqtol וַיַּגַּע and speaks. In the speech, the coal has touched your lips and two clauses follow: וְסָר עֲוֺנֶךָ, 'your guilt departs', and a second clause with a passive verb, תְּכֻפָּר, with no agent named.

examples.analysis: וָאֶשְׁמַע is again a first person wayyiqtol. The LORD asks two questions with מִי, the first with a first person yiqtol (אֶשְׁלַח), the second with a third person (יֵלֶךְ). Isaiah answers הִנְנִי, 'here I am', and the imperative with a suffix, שְׁלָחֵנִי, 'send me'.

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: and he touched my mouth with it, and said: Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin expiated.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The verb is passive: your sin is covered or atoned for, and no agent is named
The subject causes someone else to act
check.explain: Pual is the passive of the Piel. The subject, וְחַטָּאתְךָ, 'your sin', receives the action. The text does not say who acts.

quoted.title: Isaiah
quoted.english: And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said: 'Here am I; send me.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Send me: an imperative with the suffix for 'me'
check.explain: The verb is an imperative of שָׁלַח, and the suffix -ֵנִי is 'me'. Isaiah answers the LORD's question 'whom shall I send' with 'here I am; send me'.

reading.why: A complete first person vision report in eight verses: long descriptive sentences with participles, a song with a nominal clause, rare words, first person wayyiqtol verbs, a passive verb with no agent, and the prophet's answer. Its commoner words are gathered in the table.
